posts.title: Notes from a Bangkok Rooftop
posts.excerpt: Three days in and the city still hadn't stopped moving.
content: The rooftop bar was four flights up a staircase that smelled like frying garlic, and none of us had made a reservation. We got in anyway, squeezed onto a bench meant for four, and watched the city do its evening thing — tuk-tuks weaving under strings of lit-up temples, the Chao Phraya going gold and then grey.
Someone ordered a mango sticky rice we didn't need and ate anyway. Nobody checked their phone for almost an hour, which for this group is basically a miracle.

I keep trying to describe Bangkok to people back home and I keep failing. It's not the temples, though they're extraordinary. It's the way the whole city seems to be running two speeds at once — frantic in the streets, unbothered on the rooftops. I think I needed both speeds more than I realized.

posts.title: The Smell of Wet Earth
posts.excerpt: Bengaluru's first rain always takes me back to the same balcony.
content: There's a smell right before the first real monsoon rain hits — petrichor, technically, though nobody in my house ever called it that. We just called it 'the smell,' and when it drifted in through the kitchen window my grandmother would stop whatever she was doing and go stand on the balcony.

I was maybe eight the first time she pulled me out there with her, both of us getting sprinkled on, watching the dry red mud in the compound go dark and shining. She told me the smell meant the earth was finally getting to breathe again after months of holding its breath.

I still go stand on my balcony for it, twenty-some years later, in a flat she's never seen. It doesn't feel like nostalgia exactly. It feels like she's still doing the telling and I'm still doing the listening.

posts.title: Why Does Everyone Walk So Slowly
posts.excerpt: A short, unhinged case for footpath etiquette.
content: I need to talk about the group of four people who insist on walking exactly shoulder to shoulder across the entire width of a footpath, at the pace of a Sunday stroll through a botanical garden, while I am trying to get to a meeting.

I have made peace with a lot of things. Traffic. Bad wifi. The fact that autocorrect thinks I mean 'ducking' when I very much do not. But I have not made peace with this, and I don't think I ever will.

There is a simple rule. If someone is clearly walking faster than you and trying to get around, you leave a gap. That's it. That's the whole rule. I'm not asking for much. I'm asking for six inches and a moment of spatial awareness.

posts.title: Getting Lost in a Night Market
posts.excerpt: No map, no plan, and the best noodles of the trip.
content: We told ourselves we'd just look around for twenty minutes. Ninety minutes and one very full stomach later, we still hadn't found our way back to the main road, and honestly none of us were trying that hard.

The market ran three lanes deep — grilled skewers on one side, some kind of shaved ice with too many toppings to name on the other, and in between, a woman selling noodles from a cart she'd clearly been running from the same spot for decades. She didn't speak much English. We didn't speak much Thai. She pointed at three options, we nodded at all three, and it remains one of the best meals of my life.
I've started to think getting a little lost on purpose is the whole point of going somewhere new. The plans you make in advance are never the ones you remember.
